newsitem.title: BRAZIL: No Brazil credit curbs seen today, but soon.
newsitem.headline: No Brazil credit curbs seen today, but soon.

text.p: Policy-makers will probably choose not to adopt stiffer credit measures at a meeting of the National Monetary Council on Thursday, but economists said new restrictions would likely come in about three weeks.
Economists said the government is contemplating further credit tightening to curb import growth and slow Brazil's widening trade deficit.
But they said there was no point in adopting new measures until after the May 11 Mother's Day holiday.

"Mothers' Day is the second largest sales event in Brazil after Christmas, but imports (for Mothers' Day) have already been ordered so new creidt restrictions would not have any effect," said Marcelo Allain, chief economist at BMC Bank in Brazil.

Economic Policy Secretary Jose Roberto Mendonca de Barros told reporters last night that no new measures would come at today's National Monetary Council, where Central Bank, Finance and Planning Ministry officials meet each month to discuss economic policy.

Also, Brazil's leading financial newspaper Gazeta Mercantil said that a Central Bank report, made public accidentally and showing weaker-than-expected credit growth of 1.9 percent in March, could make officials think additional credit restrictions were unnecessary for the time being.

But economists said the government was growing increasingly concerned about the trade deficit -- expected to top $10 billion this year from $5.5 billion in 1996 -- which has surged despite modest economic and credit growth.

"These new measures will have much more to do with trade than economic activity, which is not overheating. We don't see measures coming today but they don't have to wait until next month's policy-making meeting to move," said Guilherme Abbud, an economist at ING Bank in Brazil.
Economists said the government would move cautiously to restrict credit, targeting durable goods, electronics and autos. They said the most likely restrictions would be limiting installment payments.
Interest rate hikes or increasing bank reserve requirements were considered too harsh at this point, analysts said.
"The government wants to reduce demand for certain products, it doesn't want to slow growth," BMC's Allain said.
